title: Photoroom's Data Lesson: Caption Quality Rivals Architecture
hook: Photoroom re-captioned their pretraining set with a VLM — longer, more accurate captions moved image FID from 21 to 13, a bigger jump than most architecture changes deliver.
key_points: Prioritizes data diversity over perfection: assembles public and internal sources, then re-captions everything with a VLM (Qwen3-VL-8B).
Long, accurate captions that describe everything in the image dramatically improve model quality — Qwen2.5-VL-style captions hit FID ~13 versus ~21 for shorter alternatives.
Uses Lance for exploratory data work and Mosaic Data Shards for efficient distributed training.
Practical mechanisms — skip-lists for filtering, perceptual-hash deduplication — let the pipeline stay flexible without destructively rewriting datasets.
content_html: It's tempting to assume the biggest gains in a training pipeline come from architecture. Photoroom's data-strategy writeup makes a case for the opposite: for their image-generation pretraining, caption quality was the highest-leverage lever they pulled.
extra_html: The approach prioritizes diversity over perfection: pull together public and internal sources, then re-caption everything with a vision-language model (Qwen3-VL-8B) rather than trusting whatever captions came attached. The headline result is a concrete before/after — long, accurate captions that describe everything in the image moved image-quality FID from around 21 with shorter captions to around 13 with Qwen2.5-VL-style long captions, a swing larger than many architecture tweaks deliver. On the engineering side, the team uses Lance for exploratory data work and Mosaic Data Shards for efficient distributed training, and favors non-destructive filtering mechanisms — skip-lists and perceptual-hash deduplication — over rewriting datasets outright, keeping the pipeline flexible as requirements change. The broader lesson for anyone building a training pipeline: caption/label quality can rival architecture choices as a lever, and it's usually cheaper to pull. Hugging Face Blog (Photoroom), 2026-07-06.

related.title: LAION-5B: Open Image-Text at Scale
related.hook: CLIP and DALL-E showed huge, noisy image-text data is gold. LAION-5B made that public — billions of CLIP-filtered pairs anyone can train open models on.

related.title: Deduplicating Training Data Makes LMs Better
related.hook: Training corpora are full of copies — one 61-word sentence shows up 60,000+ times in C4. Strip the duplicates and models memorize far less and evaluate more honestly.

related.title: Moving Alphabet: A Controlled Study of Training Data for Text-to-Video Generation
related.hook: Text-to-video research chases bigger architectures; this controlled study shows the training data decides the outcome — caption quality alone can cap what the model learns.

flashcards.prompt: What single data change gave Photoroom the biggest quality jump in their pretraining pipeline?
flashcards.back_html: Re-captioning their entire dataset with a VLM using long, accurate captions that describe everything in the image — moving FID from about 21 (short captions) to about 13.

flashcards.prompt: Why does Photoroom avoid destructive operations in their data pipeline (favoring skip-lists and hash-based dedup over rewriting datasets)?

choices.text: It keeps the pipeline flexible so it can adapt as requirements evolve, without needing to regenerate the whole dataset each time
Destructive operations are technically impossible with their storage format
It saves on GPU compute during training, unrelated to flexibility
Regulatory requirements mandate keeping all original data untouched

flashcards.explanation_html: Non-destructive filtering (skip-lists, perceptual-hash dedup) lets the team change what's included without rewriting the underlying dataset — a flexibility that pays off as data requirements shift over time.
